name: The Class for Representing a Point in the Euclidean Plane (Case 1)
description: Construct a class that represents a point in the Euclidean plane. The class should contain data that represents the point’s integer coordinates (x,y). The point's coordinates could be accessed or changed only through the getter and setter methods. The class should also include a method to translate the point, i.e., shift the point's location by the specified amount.
code:
#Step 1: Define the class
class Point1 :
    #Step 1.1: Declare the method to shift the location of the point by the given amount
    def translate(self, dx, dy) :
        self.__x += dx
        self.__y += dy
    #Step 1.2: Define the setter and getter methods for the x-coordinate of the point
    def set_x(self, new_x) :
        self.__x = new_x
    def get_x(self) :
        return self.__x
    #Step 1.3: Define the setter and getter methods for the y-coordinate of the point
    def set_y(self, new_y) :
        self.__y = new_y
    def get_y(self) :
        return self.__y
#Step 2: Test the class
p1 = Point1()
p1.set_x(7)
p1.set_y(2)
p1.translate(11, 6)
print("p1 coordinates: (" + str(p1.get_x()) + ", " + str(p1.get_y()) + ")")

commentList: You can see this line prints the point's coordinates to the console by building a single text string that includes the values returned by p1.get_x() and p1.get_y(); it shows the point's final location after translate was called.

Syntax breakdown: you call print(...). Inside the parentheses you use string concatenation with + to join the literal parts (like 'p1 coordinates: (', ', ', ')') and the coordinate values. The calls str(p1.get_x()) and str(p1.get_y()) convert the integers into strings so they can be concatenated.

What happens at runtime: first p1.get_x() and p1.get_y() are invoked to fetch the integer coordinates, then str(...) converts each integer to text, then + joins all pieces into one string (for example 'p1 coordinates: (18, 8)'), and finally print displays that string.

Potential errors and misconceptions: if you remove the str(...) calls and try to join integers to strings with +, you'll get a TypeError because Python won't concatenate ints and strs. Also, if you never initialized __x or __y (no __init__ and you didn't call set_x/set_y before), calling get_x/get_y could raise an AttributeError.

Best practices: you should initialize attributes in an __init__ method so the getters always work. For clearer and safer formatting prefer an f-string, e.g. print(f'p1 coordinates: ({p1.get_x()}, {p1.get_y()})'), or implement __repr__ in the class to print the object directly.

Formatting alternatives you might try: you can use commas in print like print('p1 coordinates:', '(', p1.get_x(), ',', p1.get_y(), ')'), but note that will insert extra spaces automatically — f-strings give you precise control over spacing and readability.

distractors.description: You might choose this because naming parameters x and y seems natural: they match the idea of coordinates. But in this program the method body refers to dx and dy. If you only change the signature to use x and y and leave the body unchanged, Python will raise a NameError when it reaches dx (or dy) because those names don't exist. Step by step: the method will receive the values in x and y, but the subsequent lines try to update using dx and dy, so the code fails at runtime. Even if you mentally think x/y match the attributes, the real problem is inconsistency between parameter names and their use in the method. This distractor is plausible because it's a harmless-looking rename, yet it breaks the program unless you also update the method body to use the same names.

You might pick this because it seems to put dx into the x field, and you might think that sets the new x value after translation. If you use this line, the method will overwrite the x coordinate with dx instead of adjusting it by dx. For example, if x was 7 and dx is 11, after this line x becomes 11 (not 18). The point ends up at the wrong location because you replaced the coordinate instead of shifting it. The program still runs, but the semantics are wrong: translate no longer means "move by dx" but rather "set x to dx". This misunderstanding comes from mixing up assignment with increment; the operation you wrote removes the previous coordinate's contribution entirely.

You might pick this because it looks like it updates the y-coordinate and uses the += operator correctly. The subtle issue is that the class uses a double-underscore name (a name-mangled private attribute), so writing self.y refers to a completely different attribute than the one your getters and setters use. If you use this line, Python will create or update a public attribute named 'y' while the original private storage remains unchanged; your get_y() will still return the old value and the translate will appear to have no effect when you inspect the point via the provided methods. There is no syntax error, which makes this a sneaky bug: it appears to work but the class invariants are broken. This distractor fails because it doesn't modify the same internal field that the rest of the class relies on.
